back: A word that tells us more about a verb, an adjective or another adverb: how, when, where, how often or to what degree.

front: Adverbs with the same form as adjectives
back: hard, fast, late, early, straight, high, far.
notes: hardly (= almost not) and lately (= recently) have different meanings.

back: well: She is a good singer; she sings well.
notes: 'She sings good' is incorrect in standard English.

back: Manner (how), time (when), place (where), frequency (how often), degree (how much), reason (why).
notes: carefully, tomorrow, outside, often, extremely, therefore.

back: Before the main verb (She often visits Gogo) but after be (He is always late) and after the first helping verb (I have never seen it).
When never, seldom, hardly, rarely or no sooner begins a sentence, the helping verb comes before the subject.
notes: Never have I seen ...; Hardly had we arrived when ...; No sooner had she left than ...

back: A subordinate clause that works like an adverb, showing time, place, reason, condition, concession, purpose or result.
notes: when the bell rang; because it rained; unless you hurry; although she was tired.

back: friendly, lovely, lonely, elderly, costly, ugly, silly are adjectives, not adverbs.
notes: Say 'in a friendly way', not 'friendly' after a verb.
